While we maintain security measures, conduct background checks where applicable, and provide training and reporting mechanisms, we cannot predict or prevent all incidents.

An incident of workplace violence could result in employee injuries, legal claims, and increased security costs. It could also disrupt business operations, lead to temporary closure of facilities, and require management and staffing resources to respond to investigations and remediation.

We could also face increased turnover if employees perceive our facilities or processes as unsafe, which would compound staffing challenges. In addition, some security-related measures may require capital expenditures or increased spending on third-party security personnel.

Although we take steps designed to mitigate these risks, workplace violence and security events could adversely affect our business and results of operations.

If we experience delays in filling leadership positions or cannot secure candidates with the required experience, our ability to manage priorities, maintain controls, and execute strategic initiatives could be impaired. Leadership transitions may also lead to changes in organizational priorities, management processes, and reporting lines, which can affect employee alignment and productivity.

Furthermore, in a competitive labor market, candidates for senior roles may have multiple opportunities, which can increase the time required to close searches and elevate compensation costs. If we appoint leaders without sufficient domain expertise, we may face increased execution risk.

We may also need to change organizational structures to improve performance, which can create uncertainty and require additional training for new leaders and managers. If our managers do not adopt consistent approaches to coaching and performance management, employee development may suffer, increasing turnover.

Any inability to maintain stable, qualified leadership and effective succession processes could adversely affect our operations and financial condition.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Compliance Training and Employee Accountability

Our compliance framework includes training, codes of conduct, and internal reporting channels. Nevertheless, compliance training effectiveness can decline if employees do not complete modules timely, if training does not reflect evolving requirements, or if employee workloads limit their participation.

When compliance responsibilities are unclear or when employees are not properly supervised, mistakes can occur. In some cases, repeated noncompliance by a subgroup of employees can indicate a broader cultural or process breakdown. If we fail to address these issues promptly, the risk of regulatory inquiries, employment-related allegations, and additional corrective actions increases.

We also rely on managers to enforce standards and to conduct periodic reviews. If management is distracted by operational demands, reviews may be less frequent or less thorough, and accountability gaps could develop.

Further, any adverse employment matter, such as a complaint involving workplace harassment or discrimination, could require remediation and additional training for affected teams. Such activities may increase costs and temporarily reduce capacity.

While we continually seek to strengthen our compliance training and oversight, we cannot assure that employees will consistently adhere to our policies, and any failure could adversely impact our operations and financial results.

Labor disputes could increase our costs and reduce our flexibility to allocate resources during peak demand periods. Any significant disruptions could impair our ability to fulfill customer orders, negatively affect revenue, and increase operating expenses.

risk_heading: Risks From Wage and Benefit Cost Increases and Compliance With Wage-and-Hour Laws

Our costs may increase due to higher minimum wages, prevailing wage requirements, benefit cost inflation, and wage adjustments driven by labor market competition. Wage-and-hour rules can also change, and we must comply with overtime, meal and rest break, classification, and recordkeeping requirements under federal and state laws.

If we fail to accurately classify employees, properly track time, or meet reporting and payroll obligations, we may be subject to back pay, penalties, and wage-and-hour litigation. Collective bargaining agreements and local labor ordinances may further constrain our ability to manage labor costs. In addition, new requirements relating to paid leave and health coverage could increase our ongoing expenses.

Any material increase in labor costs, combined with reduced ability to pass cost increases to customers, could compress margins. Compliance issues can also disrupt operations due to audits, corrective action plans, and management attention devoted to remediation. These outcomes could adversely affect our financial results.

In addition, if we rely more heavily on temporary workers or external service providers during demand surges, training and supervision requirements may increase and the likelihood of human error can rise. Compliance with internal procedures and documentation may also degrade when teams are understaffed.

We have implemented quality management processes and standard operating procedures designed to reduce errors, but these controls may not prevent all incidents. Any significant increase in defect rates, rework, or safety events caused by inadequate training or operational mistakes could negatively affect our ability to satisfy customer requirements and could result in additional costs or claims.

Public health events may also impact employee mental wellbeing and engagement, leading to increased turnover after a disruption. We may also face challenges ensuring that contractor personnel comply with relevant health and safety guidance. risk_heading: Risks Related to Use of Third-Party Contractors and Supply-Chain Labor Practices

A supplier labor issue, such as unlawful practices or workplace hazards, could lead to production delays, termination of supplier relationships, or increased costs as we qualify alternative sources.

In addition, contractor turnover or staffing shortages can negatively affect quality, customer satisfaction, and continuity of service. If we fail to manage contractor performance and training, we may experience operational errors, employee disputes, or increased claims related to workplace conditions.

Any significant deficit in plan funding could also increase the risk of plan constraints imposed by regulators or counterparties.

These factors may adversely affect our financial condition and the ability to attract and retain employees, particularly in competitive markets where benefits are a key component of total compensation.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Workforce Restructuring and Change Management
paragraph_text:

Restructuring can involve headcount reductions, changes in job functions, consolidation of facilities, and modifications to compensation plans. Such actions are inherently disruptive and require careful change management to maintain employee morale and operational continuity.

Even if restructuring is planned and compliant, it can trigger employee claims related to discrimination, wrongful termination, wage issues, or failure to follow established policies. During the transition period, key employees may leave before their roles are fully integrated, which can delay critical projects and weaken institutional knowledge. In addition, remaining employees may experience increased workloads and burnout, potentially reducing productivity and increasing the likelihood of errors.

We may also need to coordinate with unions, works councils, or regulatory bodies in certain jurisdictions. If we do not execute restructuring effectively, we could incur higher-than-expected costs, including severance, retention incentives, and training for replacement roles.

Any disruption caused by workforce restructuring could adversely affect our operating results and our ability to deliver services to customers.

We seek to maintain uniform policies and provide training for managers; however, actual practices can vary, particularly in high-growth periods when new leaders are added quickly.

Any failure to effectively manage staffing transitions could adversely affect our customer relationships and results of operations.

risk_heading: Risks From Employee Misclassification and Independent Contractor Controls
paragraph_text:
We utilize independent contractors and contingent workers for certain specialized services, which can provide flexibility. However, regulators continue to scrutinize the classification of workers as independent contractors versus employees. Misclassification can result in payment of back taxes, penalties, and liabilities for unpaid wages or benefits, as well as increased risk of employment-related litigation.

Our ability to comply depends on accurate documentation and consistent application of criteria regarding control over work, scheduling, and equipment usage. In practice, the work performed by contingent workers may evolve over time, and managers may adjust processes to meet operational needs. These operational changes can complicate classification assessments if our internal controls do not keep pace.

In addition, if contractors are not provided with appropriate training on workplace procedures and security protocols, risks of operational disruptions or safety incidents may increase. We may also need to provide contractors with additional protections or adjust contractor engagement models if required by law.

Any material misclassification issues or subsequent remediation could increase operating costs, limit our use of contingent labor, and disrupt service delivery.

If suppliers experience labor-related interruptions, we may not be able to quickly source alternative capacity, particularly for specialized components with limited qualified vendors. In addition, increased enforcement or new requirements from customers and regulators could increase our compliance costs and require more frequent audits or remediation plans. Any failure to manage supply-chain labor risks could adversely affect our operations and financial performance.

risk_heading: Risks From Health and Safety Compliance in High-Risk Facilities
paragraph_text:
We operate facilities that involve industrial processes, maintenance of heavy equipment, and periodic work by contractors. These activities create inherent health and safety risks, including exposure to chemicals, lockout/tagout failures, energized equipment hazards, and confined-space dangers. Even with engineered safeguards and written procedures, incidents may occur due to human error, equipment malfunction, or failure to follow protocols.

Changes in workplace safety regulations, inspection intensity, or enforcement practices could increase the likelihood of citations, fines, or required remediation. If we are required to modify equipment, change operating procedures, or reduce throughput to address safety issues, our costs could increase and production schedules may be impacted.

In addition, contractor management poses risks. Contractors may have different safety cultures, training backgrounds, or maintenance practices. If we cannot effectively verify contractor compliance and ensure coordination between our personnel and contractors, accidents could result.

We perform safety audits and maintain training requirements; however, we cannot assure that we will avoid serious incidents. A significant safety event could also lead to workforce disruptions, investigations, and difficulty recruiting or retaining employees willing to work at high-risk facilities.

Required funding increases could reduce cash available for investments in growth initiatives or operational improvements. We also face risks associated with benefit administration, including errors in eligibility determinations, enrollment records, or plan communications. Employee dissatisfaction with benefit outcomes could contribute to turnover or lead to disputes.

We manage these risks through governance processes and periodic reviews of actuarial factors, but we cannot assure that market movements, regulatory changes, or participant behaviors will not adversely affect our obligations. risk_heading: Risks Related to Employee Data Privacy and HR System Management
paragraph_text:
We maintain systems and processes that collect and store employee-related information, including payroll data, health-related accommodations, and performance records. These records are valuable and may be targeted through cyber incidents or may be exposed due to inadvertent employee actions, misconfigured access controls, or inadequate training.

While data privacy and cybersecurity risks are discussed elsewhere in our filings, the human capital dimension is significant because improper handling by personnel—such as sharing confidential information, failing to follow approved workflows, or incorrectly granting system permissions—can lead to privacy violations and employment-related disputes. If employees’ personal or medical information is improperly accessed or disclosed, we could face regulatory inquiries, legal claims, and additional compliance obligations.

We implement access controls, audit logging, and security awareness training for personnel with system access. However, the effectiveness of these measures depends on consistent use by employees and administrators. Frequent system enhancements, integration of new HR tools, and evolving roles can increase the likelihood of process errors.

Any breach or persistent weaknesses in HR system management could result in remediation costs, impacts to employee trust, and increased turnover. These events could adversely affect our ability to retain talent and execute operational priorities.

risk_heading: Risks From Organizational Changes and Restructuring
paragraph_text:
From time to time, we may implement restructuring actions, including workforce reductions, consolidation of functions, or changes in operating models. Restructuring is intended to improve efficiency and align resources, but it can also create uncertainty for employees and disrupt the continuity of operations. Reduced morale, loss of institutional knowledge, and difficulty retaining high-performing employees can occur during transitional periods.

Restructuring may require negotiating with labor organizations, updating job classifications, and managing employee benefits obligations. Even when actions are implemented in accordance with applicable laws, employee concerns may lead to increased litigation risk or regulatory scrutiny. Additionally, changes to reporting lines and responsibilities can create operational inefficiencies if roles are not clearly defined and employees are not sufficiently trained for new responsibilities.

If restructuring results in diminished productivity or delays in execution of strategic initiatives, our ability to meet customer commitments could be impaired. Moreover, a reduction in workforce capability may make it more challenging to address urgent operational issues such as production interruptions, quality investigations, or customer escalations.

We mitigate these risks through transition planning and communications, but we cannot assure that restructuring efforts will not adversely affect our workforce stability and operating performance.

risk_heading: Risks Associated With Employee Claims and Workplace Disputes

Such claims can be costly to defend and may require changes to policies, management practices, or staffing structures. Even when we believe allegations are unfounded, the cost of investigations, legal fees, and potential settlements can be significant.

Workplace disputes may also arise from restructuring, changing performance metrics, compensation adjustments, or disputes over workplace assignments and scheduling. If managers do not apply performance standards consistently, employees may perceive unfairness and pursue formal complaints. We rely on management judgment and training to apply policies; however, inconsistent application may occur across locations and business units.

We have internal human resources and compliance functions designed to investigate complaints and support consistent practices. However, investigation processes may take time, and outcomes are uncertain. Additionally, repeated employee disputes could negatively affect culture and engagement, increasing the risk of attrition among high performers.

Any material increase in employment litigation, regulatory findings, or settlement costs could adversely affect our operating results and reputation as an employer of choice.

risk_heading: Risks From Inadequate Knowledge Transfer During System and Process Changes
paragraph_text:
We regularly update internal systems and operational processes, including planning tools, manufacturing execution platforms, and customer order workflows. Implementing these changes often requires retraining employees and documenting new procedures. If employees do not fully adopt the updated systems or if training materials are incomplete, we may experience operational errors.

For example, during transitions to new scheduling and inventory planning tools, employees may use incorrect data fields, resulting in forecasting errors, missed replenishment, or delayed shipments. Similarly, process changes related to quality inspections may be misunderstood, leading to inconsistent acceptance decisions. While the underlying causes may be technical, human factors—including limited training time and reliance on “tribal knowledge”—can increase the probability of error.

We manage change through training, phased rollouts, and increased supervision during go-live periods. However, resource constraints may limit the ability to provide sufficient training across all shifts and locations. Additionally, if employees are distracted by concurrent initiatives or staffing shortages, adoption may be incomplete.

Any material increase in operational errors or delays due to inadequate knowledge transfer could adversely affect our customer commitments, increase costs for rework, and impact our ability to meet financial targets.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Recruiting and Retaining Specialized Technical Skills

Hiring in these disciplines can be time-consuming and costly, and in certain regions the market may be highly competitive. If we cannot recruit qualified candidates on a timely basis, we may need to extend project timelines or reduce the scope of new initiatives.

Retention challenges may also arise if competitors offer more attractive compensation structures, enhanced benefits, remote-work flexibility, or faster career progression. Differences in compensation benchmarking could result in internal pay compression that employees perceive as unfair, increasing the risk of turnover among critical roles.

We use training programs, mentorship, and internal mobility to build skills, but these initiatives require time and may not fully substitute for immediate hiring needs. In addition, use of contractors to bridge skill gaps may introduce quality and oversight risks if deliverables are not adequately reviewed.

Any inability to attract and retain the talent necessary for our strategic roadmap could impair our capacity to develop and support products and services, potentially resulting in lower revenue growth and higher operating costs.

risk_heading: Risks from Workforce Reorganization and Restructuring
paragraph_text:

Restructuring can create disruption, including the loss of institutional knowledge, delays in implementation, and challenges integrating new teams or vendors. Employee morale may be negatively affected, which can reduce productivity and increase voluntary turnover.

If labor laws or collective bargaining obligations require consultation, severance, or other procedural steps, restructuring timelines may extend and costs may increase. Additionally, we may face claims or grievances related to termination practices, classification of employees, or alleged discrimination. Even if such claims are ultimately resolved in our favor, the process can be costly and can divert management attention.

We also rely on trained personnel to operate critical systems and equipment. When positions are eliminated or responsibilities are reallocated, the remaining employees may experience increased workload and training gaps, which can raise the likelihood of operational errors and safety incidents.

There can be no assurance that our workforce planning and restructuring efforts will achieve intended savings or performance improvements, and any failure could adversely affect our results of operations and ability to compete.

risk_heading: Compliance Risks Related to Wage and Hour Practices
paragraph_text:
Our businesses are subject to federal, state, and local wage and hour, overtime, and workplace classification requirements. These rules can be complex and are periodically revised through regulation, administrative guidance, or court decisions. Misinterpretation of eligibility for overtime, exemptions, or timekeeping practices could lead to wage and hour violations.

In addition, employee expectations regarding pay transparency and fair compensation continue to evolve. If we fail to administer compensation programs consistently, employees may challenge payroll practices through agency complaints or class actions. These matters may result in the payment of back wages, penalties, attorneys’ fees, and other damages, which could be material. Even when we believe our practices comply with applicable law, litigation can consume significant resources and create operational disruption.

We rely on robust payroll systems and internal controls to manage timekeeping and compensation, including automated reporting and periodic audits. However, if there are errors in time reporting, insufficient training of managers, or system failures, we could incur liabilities. Further, changes in our workforce mix, use of temporary labor, and adoption of new scheduling methods may increase the risk of noncompliance.

Any material adverse outcome from wage and hour claims or compliance efforts could harm our financial condition and ability to attract and retain talent.

risk_heading: Supply-Chain Labor Standards and Forced Labor Risk
paragraph_text:
We depend on a global network of suppliers and subcontractors to produce components and services used in our offerings. Although we maintain policies intended to promote ethical labor practices, including codes of conduct and supplier assessments, we may not fully control the labor practices of suppliers and their sub-tier vendors. Risks may include excessive working hours, unsafe working conditions, wage withholding, child labor, or other forms of forced labor.

Economic pressures, rapid changes in demand, and supplier cost-reduction initiatives can increase the likelihood of labor violations. In some cases, suppliers may not be able or willing to provide transparency into their facilities, recruitment practices, or worker-management relationships, which can limit the effectiveness of our audits and monitoring.

If credible allegations of labor abuses arise, we may be required to investigate, remediate, or suspend or terminate supplier relationships. Such actions could increase costs, disrupt supply continuity, or require requalification of alternative suppliers, which can delay production and deliveries. Regulatory enforcement and customer requirements may also expand, increasing our compliance obligations.

While we seek to reduce these risks through contractual requirements and training for relevant teams, we cannot assure that our actions will prevent labor-related issues. Any failure to identify or address labor standards risks could adversely affect our reputation and financial results.

risk_heading: Employee Misconduct Allegations and Workplace Culture Risks

Misconduct—such as harassment, discrimination, retaliation, theft, or violations of workplace policies—may occur despite training and our code of conduct. In addition, remote and hybrid work arrangements can complicate supervision and increase the likelihood of isolated incidents that are not detected promptly.

When allegations arise, we may need to conduct investigations and provide accommodations or remediate identified issues. These activities can be time-consuming and may require outside legal or investigative support. From time to time, we update policies and training materials in response to developments in law and employee feedback. However, we cannot guarantee that these efforts will prevent misconduct or ensure consistent enforcement across geographies and business units.

Any material adverse outcome from misconduct claims, regulatory findings, or reputational harm could adversely affect our ability to attract and retain employees and could impact our operating performance.

Our security posture depends on the effectiveness of ongoing training, monitoring, and access management. Any material breach or failure in our human-controlled processes could adversely affect our reputation and financial results. Although we strive to minimize these risks, there is no assurance that our controls will be effective in preventing all incidents.

Additionally, when seasonal demand increases, we may rely on temporary staff who require onboarding and supervision. If supervisors are stretched, new workers may not receive adequate coaching.

Any material increase in errors, compliance issues, or workplace incidents attributable to training and competency gaps could adversely affect our financial results and ability to maintain customer trust.

risk_heading: Retention and Safety Risks from Contractor Dependence
paragraph_text:

While we select contractors based on experience and require compliance with our safety and conduct standards, contractors may not be as familiar with our processes, quality requirements, or reporting obligations as our employees.

If contractor staffing levels are reduced, contractors are reassigned, or key contractors leave abruptly, we may face delays or increased costs to replace them on short notice. In addition, contractor turnover can lead to inconsistent execution of procedures, which may raise the likelihood of workplace incidents and customer service disruptions.

We seek to manage these risks through onboarding, periodic performance reviews, and required completion of safety courses before working on site. However, contractor scheduling and the varying capabilities of different providers can make it difficult to ensure uniform standards. During peak demand periods, we may increase contractor utilization, heightening the risk that supervision is insufficient and that tasks are performed by less experienced individuals.

Any material safety incident involving contractors, inability to meet service timelines, or failure to control contractor compliance could adversely affect our operations and expose us to claims and penalties.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Aging Workforce and Succession Planning
paragraph_text:
A portion of our workforce is concentrated among employees with specialized experience, and we face increasing retirements over the coming years. As more employees reach eligibility for retirement, we must transfer institutional knowledge to less experienced personnel. If succession planning is insufficient, we may experience delays in maintaining capabilities in engineering, regulatory affairs, and skilled trades positions.

The transition of knowledge may be complicated by complex processes that are not fully documented and by reliance on on-the-job experience. New personnel may require extended training, and productivity may decline during ramp-up periods. In addition, we may face challenges in recruiting replacements in certain locations where specialized labor markets are limited.

We attempt to mitigate these risks through knowledge management initiatives, mentorship programs, and internal development plans. However, these efforts may not fully address operational gaps if retirements occur faster than anticipated or if employees do not stay through planned handover periods.

Any material inability to staff critical roles or maintain operational continuity could adversely affect our manufacturing, customer support capabilities, and ability to execute strategic projects.

risk_heading: Failure to Maintain Adequate Workforce Scheduling and Coverage

Scheduling requirements may change due to seasonal demand, unexpected service volume, customer cancellations, or new regulatory reporting obligations that require additional personnel. If we fail to staff adequately, we could experience service backlogs, reduced customer responsiveness, and increased overtime costs.

Conversely, overstaffing may increase fixed labor expenses and reduce flexibility, which can become challenging during demand slowdowns. In both cases, the mismatch between labor supply and business needs can lead to inefficiencies and increased risk of employee fatigue. Excessive overtime can also increase the likelihood of safety incidents and errors, which may require additional training or remedial actions.

We use forecasting, scheduling software, and cross-training to manage coverage. However, forecasts may be inaccurate, and scheduling systems may not account for real-time disruptions such as transportation delays or sudden employee absences. Cross-trained employees may not be able to fully substitute for specialized roles on short notice.

If we cannot maintain effective scheduling and coverage, we may be unable to meet contract obligations and may face penalties or loss of business. Such outcomes could have an adverse effect on our results of operations.

risk_heading: Supply-Chain Labor Practices and Third-Party Workforce Risk
paragraph_text:
We depend on third-party suppliers and manufacturers for certain components and services. Although we require our suppliers to comply with applicable labor and human rights laws, including restrictions on forced labor and child labor, we may not be able to fully verify labor practices across complex, multi-tier supply chains. Subcontracting, informal work arrangements, and limited transparency in certain regions can hinder our ability to detect non-compliance in a timely manner.

If suppliers fail to meet labor standards, we could face reputational harm, loss of business opportunities, and potential regulatory actions. In addition, labor disputes at supplier sites could disrupt delivery schedules, resulting in production delays and increased costs. We may also be required to change sourcing arrangements, audit programs, or contractual terms, which could reduce flexibility and increase overhead.

We conduct audits and require corrective action plans where issues are identified; however, remediation may take time and may not prevent recurrence. Further, supplier actions to improve labor practices could increase supplier costs that we may not be able to pass through.

Failure to maintain acceptable labor standards within our supply chain or disruptions caused by labor unrest could adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations.

risk_heading: Remote Work and Human Resource Management Risks During Disruptions
paragraph_text:
We rely on a workforce that performs both in-person and remote functions. During periods of public health outbreaks, natural disasters, or other disruptions, we may shift certain roles to remote or modify workplace operations to comply with guidance issued by governmental authorities. Remote and hybrid arrangements can affect communication, supervision, and information security practices. From a human capital perspective, these arrangements can also increase employee burnout, reduce training effectiveness for new hires, and impair collaboration needed for timely project delivery.

If remote work increases attrition or reduces engagement—particularly for early-career employees—we may experience higher turnover in critical functions. In addition, we must ensure that remote employees understand their responsibilities, including policies addressing conduct, harassment reporting, and data handling. Failures in training or supervision can contribute to workplace disputes and regulatory exposure.

We may also encounter challenges in staffing facilities, including maintaining adequate coverage for essential roles and meeting labor law requirements such as attendance, timekeeping, and overtime approval.

Any inability to adapt our workforce model effectively during disruptions, or increased employee dissatisfaction and turnover, could negatively affect our operations, productivity, and results.

risk_heading: Risks Associated With Pension and Retirement Plan Obligations
paragraph_text:
We sponsor retirement and other postemployment benefit plans for eligible employees, including defined benefit and defined contribution arrangements. Changes in interest rates, asset returns, inflation, and actuarial assumptions can affect plan funded status and our required contributions. While these risks have both financial and actuarial components, deteriorating plan funding can also impact employee perceptions of job security and may create additional negotiation pressures in collective bargaining or restructuring activities.

If we are required to make additional contributions to underfunded plans, cash resources may be reduced and could affect investment priorities. In addition, employees may elect benefit options that change the timing and amount of future payouts.

In some cases, employees may be eligible for withdrawal or termination-related benefits if we restructure or if a plan is frozen or modified. If regulatory agencies or plan participants challenge plan design changes, we may be required to reinstate benefit terms or make additional contributions.

Any significant adverse changes in plan funding, regulatory requirements, or participant actions could increase our costs and affect our ability to attract and retain employees, particularly where pension benefits are an important part of total compensation.

risk_heading: Employee Misconduct Allegations and Workplace Investigations
paragraph_text:
We maintain policies and procedures intended to prevent misconduct, including harassment, discrimination, retaliation, and violations of workplace rules. Nevertheless, allegations of misconduct can arise. When they occur, we may initiate internal investigations, involve third-party counsel, and implement corrective actions. Investigations can be resource-intensive and may require temporarily removing employees from roles or adjusting reporting lines, which can affect operational continuity.

If allegations involve senior employees or individuals managing teams, we could experience increased turnover or difficulty maintaining effective leadership. In addition, misconduct allegations can lead to legal proceedings, regulatory inquiries, and potential settlements. Even where outcomes are favorable, the costs associated with investigation, legal defense, and remediation may be significant.

We also face risks associated with ensuring that managers apply policies consistently. Manager behavior and decision-making can influence the workplace environment and affect employee trust in reporting mechanisms. Failure to respond appropriately to allegations could result in further claims, including constructive discharge or failure-to-accommodate theories.

Any workplace misconduct allegations, if not handled effectively, could adversely affect our reputation, employee morale, retention, and operating results.

However, monitoring and analytics tools can create employee concerns and increase the risk of disputes regarding surveillance practices. If employees believe that monitoring is intrusive, discriminatory, or used improperly, we may face claims related to wrongful termination, failure to accommodate, or violations of privacy laws.

In addition, certain monitoring systems may rely on automated decision-making, such as scheduling, performance indicators, or workforce planning. If these systems contain errors or insufficient controls, we could make adverse employment decisions based on inaccurate data. Correcting data issues can take time and may require retraining of managers and employees.

Any failure to properly administer workforce data—whether due to system malfunctions, inadequate policies, or employee misunderstanding—could result in regulatory investigations, penalties, and reputational harm. It could also affect recruitment and retention by influencing employee perceptions of workplace fairness and respect.

Accordingly, risks related to workforce data handling and employee rights could adversely affect our operations and costs.

risk_heading: Turnover and Morale Impacts from Restructuring and Cost-Cutting
paragraph_text:
From time to time, we may undertake restructurings, including reorganizing reporting lines, closing or consolidating facilities, or reducing headcount, to improve efficiency or respond to changing market conditions. While we plan these actions carefully, restructuring can create uncertainty among employees and may affect morale, productivity, and collaboration. Remaining employees may experience increased workloads, which can contribute to burnout and higher attrition.

Restructuring also requires careful handling of employment agreements, severance obligations, and benefit plans. If we do not properly comply with notice requirements, arbitration clauses, or local labor regulations, we could face employee claims or litigation. In addition, reorganizations can create operational continuity risk, such as loss of institutional knowledge or gaps in staffing during transition periods.

We may also need to adjust compensation and incentives to retain critical talent during and after a restructuring. If we are unable to retain key employees, we may not achieve projected cost savings or operational improvements.

Accordingly, the timing, cost, and operational impact of restructurings, and the related effects on employee engagement and turnover, could adversely affect our business.

risk_heading: Employee Engagement and Retention Risks in Highly Regulated Operations
paragraph_text:

We depend on our workforce to maintain compliance through adherence to documented processes, recordkeeping, and quality controls. Employee disengagement, attrition, or inadequate training can increase the likelihood of nonconformities, investigations, and corrective actions.

Regulatory bodies may require retraining, auditing, or enhanced oversight if they identify systemic issues. Such actions can consume management time and resources, and they can also lead to production downtime if critical staff are unavailable to perform required verification or quality release activities.

We also operate with staffing models that may be strained by seasonal demand. If we rely on new hires or cross-trained employees before they have adequate experience, we may face increased errors and a need to re-perform work.

Any failure to keep employees engaged, adequately trained, and retained in key functions could adversely affect our ability to meet regulatory expectations, maintain product or service performance, and protect our reputation.

We may also face compliance obligations related to documentation, reporting, and verification. Any failure to comply with work authorization requirements could lead to penalties, increased scrutiny, or restrictions on hiring.

To the extent that workforce migration and work authorization issues affect staffing continuity or increase compliance costs, our operations could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Employee Training and Competency Gaps in New Facility Openings

If we fail to align staffing and supervisory practices to local requirements, we may face claims related to scheduling, discrimination, or wage-and-hour compliance.

Any disruptions associated with hiring, training, or labor practices at new sites could delay ramp-up, increase costs, and adversely affect our results.

risk_heading: Employee Legal and Regulatory Exposure from Workplace Misclassification

Our business depends on proper classification of workers for wage-and-hour purposes, benefits eligibility, and compliance with applicable labor laws. Misclassification risks can increase where job roles evolve, supervisors use inconsistent criteria for determining overtime eligibility, or contingent workers are added quickly to respond to demand.

If regulators or claimants assert that certain workers were improperly classified, we could be liable for back wages, penalties, and interest. Misclassification disputes can also lead to class or collective actions, increasing defense costs and settlement exposure. Separately, if contingent workers are not provided appropriate training or safety information, we could face workplace injury claims.

We aim to maintain documentation supporting classifications and to train supervisors on evolving legal standards. However, these standards may change, and legal interpretations vary by jurisdiction. As a result, compliance efforts may not prevent challenges.

Any adverse outcomes related to labor misclassification could negatively impact our operations, increase costs, and harm employee relations.

risk_heading: Risks of Inadequate Succession Planning for Critical Leadership Roles
paragraph_text:
We rely on a relatively small number of leaders with deep knowledge of our strategy, operational processes, and customer relationships. While we maintain succession planning, leadership transitions—whether due to retirement, voluntary departure, illness, or termination—could occur on an accelerated timeline. If successors are not fully prepared or do not have adequate experience managing complex functions, transitions can disrupt decision-making, delay key initiatives, and affect employee confidence.

Succession risk may be heightened when we attempt to fill roles quickly during periods of growth or transformation. In these circumstances, we may rely on internal candidates who are promoted before reaching full readiness or on external candidates who must adapt to our culture, controls, and performance standards.

Leadership gaps can also affect the effectiveness of training programs, performance management, and employee relations. Employees may be more likely to disengage if they perceive instability or inconsistent leadership.

Any sustained inability to attract, develop, and retain qualified executives and senior management could adversely affect our business, including our ability to implement strategic initiatives and maintain operational continuity.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Our Workforce, Safety and Retention
paragraph_text: Our results depend on our ability to attract, develop, and retain a skilled workforce across manufacturing, warehouse and customer support operations. Employee turnover, labor shortages, and increased wage and benefits expectations could raise operating costs and reduce productivity. In addition, we rely on contractors and staffing agencies for certain functions, and their turnover and training practices may differ from those of our employees. Safety incidents, including recordable injuries and near-misses, could occur despite training and safety controls, particularly in facilities with evolving processes or rapid throughput changes. A serious injury or workplace dispute could lead to regulatory investigations, higher workers’ compensation expense, involuntary shutdowns, or restrictions on certain activities. We are also subject to changing labor and employment laws, including requirements related to overtime, scheduling, wages, and nondiscrimination. If we are unable to comply with these requirements or to manage employee relations effectively, we may face claims, higher legal costs, and reputational harm, which could adversely affect our ability to maintain service levels and meet customer demand.

risk_heading: Risks Associated With Diversity, Equal Employment Opportunity and Compensation Practices
paragraph_text: We employ a diverse workforce and operate in environments where discrimination and wage-and-hour practices are closely scrutinized. If our recruiting, promotion, performance management, or compensation practices are alleged to be unfair or noncompliant, we could face claims, administrative proceedings, or litigation. Such allegations may relate to pay equity, denial of opportunities, accommodation of disabilities, or retaliation following complaints. Even where we ultimately prevail, the cost of defending matters and the diversion of management time could be significant. Additionally, changes in federal and state regulations and evolving enforcement priorities may require us to adjust our policies and systems, including our processes for managing employee grievances and maintaining documentation. Our ability to attract and retain employees may also be impacted if candidates perceive that we do not foster an inclusive culture or if employee engagement declines. In certain jurisdictions, we are required to implement wage transparency and job classification procedures; failures or delays in these areas could result in fines and reputational harm. These issues could negatively affect productivity, labor stability, and the continuity of our operations.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Labor Practices in Our Supply Chain
paragraph_text: We depend on suppliers and logistics providers for materials, components and finished products. While we seek to contractually require responsible labor practices, our ability to monitor compliance may be limited by supplier size, geographic dispersion, and the complexity of multi-tier sourcing. If suppliers experience staffing instability, inadequate worker training, or cost-driven production pressures, there is a risk of violations of applicable labor standards, including excessive overtime, unsafe working conditions, or improper use of temporary workers. Concerns may also arise where local laws regarding wages, working hours, or labor contracting differ from our standards or are difficult to verify. Any confirmed labor-related incidents involving a supplier could lead to disrupted deliveries, increased inspection and remediation costs, termination of supplier relationships, and delays in fulfilling customer orders. In addition, such events could result in regulatory inquiries, wage restitution obligations, or claims by workers and advocacy organizations. Our brand and ability to attract employees and business partners could be harmed if stakeholders perceive that we have not effectively managed labor risks. These outcomes could adversely affect our operating results and financial condition.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Water Sourcing, Withdrawal and Treatment
paragraph_text:
We depend on reliable access to sufficient, high-quality water for manufacturing, cooling, cleaning and, in certain cases, product finishing. Water supplies in the regions where we operate may become less reliable due to drought, seasonal variability, increased competition for water, and groundwater depletion. In addition, water quality may deteriorate over time because of upstream discharges, extreme weather events or changes in hydrology. If we are required to reduce withdrawals, treat water more extensively, or incur additional costs to secure alternative supplies, our operating results could be adversely affected. Regulatory agencies may also impose withdrawal limits, require additional monitoring, or mandate upgrades to treatment systems, which could increase capital expenditures and operating expenses.

We also maintain water treatment and monitoring programs; however, these programs may not fully prevent contamination, process inefficiencies, or exceedances of applicable discharge standards. Any short-term inability to access water at required quality or quantity could disrupt production schedules, delay deliveries and trigger contractual penalties. Longer-term impacts could also increase the risk that customers and counterparties reconsider sourcing decisions based on perceived environmental performance, reputational impact and supply continuity.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Biodiversity Impacts and Habitat Protection Requirements
paragraph_text:
Some of our operations and projects require land use decisions that may affect local ecosystems and biodiversity. During facility expansions, maintenance activities, or related infrastructure work, we may need to obtain permits addressing habitat disturbance, stormwater controls, wetland impacts, and protected species protections. Changes in environmental requirements, delays in obtaining permits, or determinations that our activities could adversely affect sensitive habitats may constrain project schedules, increase costs, or require mitigation measures.

We rely on environmental studies and mitigation plans; however, field conditions can change and biological surveys may not perfectly predict future species presence, seasonal patterns or the severity of potential impacts. If agencies determine that our mitigation efforts are insufficient, we may face additional obligations, including longer-term monitoring, habitat restoration, or implementation of additional engineering controls. Mitigation expenses and associated overhead could reduce profitability.

In certain jurisdictions, community stakeholders and environmental groups may also challenge land-use approvals, increasing the likelihood of litigation or administrative appeals that could further delay construction or require redesign. These risks are particularly relevant where our facilities are located near ecologically sensitive areas or where protected species are present.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Land Contamination, Remediation Obligations and Soil Disturbance
paragraph_text:
We own, lease and operate facilities and properties that may have been used for industrial activities prior to our involvement or prior to the current use. Environmental conditions on these properties can deteriorate over time, and contamination of soil, groundwater and adjacent land may be discovered through inspections, regulatory oversight, or third-party complaints. If contamination is identified, we may be required to investigate, remediate, and monitor sites under federal, state and local environmental laws, including laws governing hazardous substance releases and corrective action.

The scope and timing of remediation activities are inherently uncertain. Remediation costs may increase materially if regulators require more aggressive methods, if contaminants are present in unexpected locations or concentrations, or if future sampling results indicate a need for additional cleanup. Moreover, certain remediation approaches may require significant excavation, demolition or off-site disposal, which can affect operations and increase capital expenditures.

We may also be exposed to claims from neighbors, remediation contractors, or governmental authorities seeking contribution for response costs. Even where we establish reserves, actual costs and liabilities could exceed expectations due to evolving regulatory standards, technology requirements, or changes in remediation timeframes. These uncertainties could adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations.

risk_heading: Risks from Sourcing Raw Materials from Water-Scarce and Biodiversity-Sensitive Regions
paragraph_text:
A portion of our supply chain depends on natural resources sourced from regions that may be exposed to water scarcity, land degradation, and ecological sensitivity. During periods of drought or heightened environmental stress, local regulators and authorities may restrict extraction, impose water-use requirements, or increase monitoring of operators. Our suppliers may also face heightened scrutiny regarding deforestation, habitat conversion, or impacts to protected species, which could result in permit denials, production interruptions, or changes to sourcing practices.

If suppliers are unable to obtain permits, maintain compliance, or meet our environmental and traceability requirements, we may experience shortages, increased input costs, or disruptions to product availability. In some cases, we may need to qualify alternative suppliers, which can require significant lead time, testing and contract renegotiations.

While we seek to mitigate these risks through supplier assessment programs, contractual environmental provisions and traceability efforts, we may not be able to fully control environmental practices across multi-tier supply chains. Data limitations, varying reporting standards and differences in enforcement can reduce the reliability of supplier assurances. Any material disruption to our ability to source environmentally acceptable inputs could adversely affect revenue, margins and customer relationships.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Compliance with Environmental Permit Conditions for Land Use and Waterway Crossings
paragraph_text:
Certain projects require permits for land use and impacts to waterways, including construction near streams, stormwater outfalls and drainage systems. Permit conditions can be complex and may include limits on construction timing, requirements for erosion and sediment controls, stormwater detention specifications, and obligations to maintain water quality. Additionally, permits may require ongoing reporting and inspections by regulators.

Permitting requirements can change as agencies update water quality standards, refine modeling methodologies, or incorporate new protective measures for local species. If we do not meet permit conditions—whether due to unforeseen site conditions, heavy rainfall beyond design assumptions, or delays in contractor performance—we could face enforcement actions, permit modifications, or suspension of work. Even where noncompliance is unintentional, corrective measures could require remediation steps, additional monitoring, or redesign of temporary works.

Because construction near waterways often involves variable terrain and hydrology, our assumptions for erosion control and drainage capacity may not always hold. Unanticipated slope failures, higher turbidity levels, or inadequate infiltration could delay milestones and increase costs. Further, any adverse environmental findings could lead to reputational harm and increased stakeholder engagement costs for future projects.

risk_heading: Risks of Inadequate Soil and Groundwater Protection During Operations
paragraph_text:
We operate facilities that involve storage and handling of industrial materials, which may pose risks to soil and groundwater if systems fail or containment is breached. While we use engineered barriers, monitoring wells, and preventative maintenance, releases can occur due to equipment malfunction, human error, or severe weather events. Climate-related increases in flooding and storm intensity may also raise the risk of overflow from secondary containment systems.

We are subject to investigations and reporting obligations under environmental laws if regulators or third parties identify potential releases. If our monitoring detects unexpected contamination, we may be required to conduct additional sampling, engage environmental consultants, and implement remedial measures. The duration and effectiveness of corrective actions may be uncertain, and groundwater cleanup efforts can require long time horizons.

Any confirmed release could result in increased remediation expenditures, decreased value of affected properties, and limitations on future use. It could also trigger liability for natural resource damages and costs to restore affected land and water. In certain cases, remediation activities may require suspending operations in whole or in part, affecting productivity and customer commitments.

Although we maintain environmental management systems and emergency response procedures, our controls may not prevent all releases or ensure timely detection and response at a scale sufficient to mitigate all impacts.

risk_heading: Risks Relating to Ecosystem Services and Watershed Management
paragraph_text:
Our facilities are located in watersheds that provide critical ecosystem services such as water filtration, flood regulation and habitat support. Activities upstream or changes in land management by other parties can alter watershed conditions and reduce the quality or availability of water we rely on. For example, increased runoff, sedimentation, or nutrient loading from agricultural or construction activities may elevate treatment costs or degrade raw water quality. In addition, watershed-scale drought conditions can reduce flows needed for certain operational requirements.

Where applicable, regulators may require us to participate in watershed management programs or adopt additional measures to protect water-related ecosystem services. Failure to comply with such requirements or an inability to implement programs effectively could result in additional oversight, increased costs, or limitations on discharges. We may also be affected by delays in permit renewals or permit modifications tied to watershed assessments.

We invest in water quality monitoring and infrastructure designed to reduce reliance on higher-cost treatment; however, these measures may not be sufficient under severe or prolonged watershed disruption. If watershed conditions deteriorate beyond our design assumptions, our ability to maintain service levels and meet customer and regulatory expectations could be impaired. Such events may adversely affect results of operations and our long-term ability to operate in certain locations.

risk_heading: Risks from Changes in Environmental Liability Standards for Natural Resource Damage
paragraph_text:
Environmental liability in the United States may extend beyond contamination of regulated media to include claims relating to natural resource damages and the restoration of affected ecosystems. If a release occurs from our operations or those of third-party contractors, we could be subject to claims by governmental agencies or other parties seeking reimbursement of assessment and restoration costs. These liabilities may arise from events that are relatively infrequent but potentially material, including spills, leaks, or other unintended discharges that impact water bodies or land.

The determination of natural resource damages can be complex and depends on technical analyses, baseline environmental conditions, the assessment of injury, and the evaluation of restoration alternatives. Methods used by regulators can evolve over time, and litigation can further influence outcomes. As a result, our estimates of potential exposure may not fully reflect future interpretations of applicable standards or the availability and cost of restoration. In addition, insurance coverage for such claims may be limited, subject to exclusions, or unavailable at commercially reasonable terms.

We mitigate these risks through safety systems, training and environmental monitoring; however, we cannot assure that these measures will be effective in preventing all incidents. Any material environmental liability, including natural resource damage claims, could adversely affect our financial condition and operating flexibility.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Coastal and Wetland Impacts from Facility and Transportation Activities
paragraph_text:
Some of our distribution and support activities involve coastal infrastructure, including loading areas, storage yards and transportation routes that may affect adjacent wetlands and coastal waters. These environments are sensitive to changes in sedimentation, turbidity, and water chemistry. Construction, dredging-related maintenance, or accidental releases could impair habitat and violate permit conditions.

Wetland and coastal permitting is often discretionary and can require mitigation for adverse impacts. If we need to expand capacity or modify infrastructure, the timing of required approvals may be influenced by seasonal constraints, agency backlog and requirements to conduct additional studies. Moreover, coastal conditions can change rapidly as a result of storms, sea-level rise, and erosion, which may create new operational constraints and increase maintenance frequency.

While we implement controls to prevent spills, manage stormwater and comply with applicable permits, we may still be exposed to enforcement actions if regulators find deviations from permit requirements. In addition, accelerated erosion could increase the likelihood of infrastructure failures, such as settlement or washouts, which could require expensive remediation.

Any significant adverse coastal or wetland impact could lead to civil penalties, reputational harm with customers and local stakeholders, and increased costs to restore affected areas.

risk_heading: Risks from Reduced Productivity Due to Water and Land Constraints
paragraph_text:
Our operations require access to usable water and stable land conditions for buildings, foundations, and utilities. Persistent drought conditions or declining groundwater availability in certain operating areas could require us to implement water rationing, substitute alternative sources, or expand treatment. These actions may increase operating expenses and reduce production capacity during periods of peak demand.

In addition, land constraints such as soil subsidence, erosion, and increased frequency of extreme precipitation events can degrade infrastructure and increase maintenance needs. For example, changes in soil moisture and repeated wetting and drying can impact pavement, storage tanks and underground piping. If infrastructure deterioration accelerates, we may need to perform repairs or replacements sooner than planned, which could require additional capital expenditures.

Government authorities could impose restrictions that limit industrial activity during drought or require enhanced land and water protection practices. Noncompliance with such restrictions could result in penalties, forced corrective actions and additional oversight.

While we maintain contingency plans and monitor local water and land conditions, we cannot predict with certainty the severity or duration of environmental disruptions. Any sustained reduction in water availability or land stability may adversely impact our ability to manufacture products on time and could materially affect financial performance.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Procurement and Certification of Environmentally Preferable Inputs
paragraph_text:
Increasing customer expectations and regulatory initiatives may require us to source certain raw materials from environmentally preferable sources. For example, customers may request documentation that inputs are produced in a manner that protects water resources, reduces land degradation and avoids conversion of sensitive habitats. Failure to meet evolving expectations may negatively affect customer relationships and the ability to renew contracts.

To address these requirements, we rely on supplier certifications, third-party audits and traceability documentation. However, certifications may not capture all environmental impacts, and audit results may not remain current as supplier operations change. In addition, supply chains may be multi-tiered, which can limit our visibility into upstream sourcing practices. Documentation may be incomplete, inaccurate or subject to fraud.

Where we elect to change suppliers or require new production practices, the transition could increase costs and create supply interruptions. Qualifying new inputs can require testing, regulatory review, and modifications to processing. Even if replacement sources are available, they may vary in quality or availability during droughts or other local environmental stresses.

We cannot assure that we will be able to procure all environmentally preferred inputs at commercially reasonable prices or in sufficient quantities. Any inability to do so could reduce our margins and adversely affect our operating results.

risk_heading: Risks from Limitations on Use of Treated Water and Discharge Constraints
paragraph_text:
Certain operations require reliance on treated water and controlled discharge of effluent. Local regulatory authorities may impose limits on volumes and concentrations, require additional treatment steps, or restrict discharge locations to protect aquatic resources. These limitations can evolve as regulators refine water-quality criteria, respond to ecological concerns, or incorporate seasonal restrictions tied to fish spawning or other sensitive periods.

If discharge constraints tighten, we may need to invest in more advanced treatment systems, increase recycling of process water, or alter production schedules to reduce effluent generation. Such changes could require significant capital expenditures and may not be completed within required timelines. In addition, operating with reduced discharge allowances could limit capacity during peak operating periods.

We monitor effluent quality and maintain treatment equipment designed to meet applicable standards; however, treatment performance may decline due to equipment aging, feedstock variability, or changes in influent characteristics. Any nonconformance could result in corrective actions, civil penalties and increased scrutiny from regulators.

Even where compliance is maintained, the cost of meeting discharge and water reuse requirements could adversely affect profitability. Furthermore, restrictions on the availability of treated water for certain internal uses could increase reliance on external sources with higher costs or lower reliability.

risk_heading: Risks of Habitat Disturbance and Increased Mitigation Costs During Facility Upgrades
paragraph_text:
From time to time, we upgrade or expand our facilities and utilities to support growth and compliance. These activities can require excavation, clearing and grading, which may disturb habitat and increase the risk of environmental impacts. Permits for these projects often require mitigation measures such as restoration of disturbed areas, relocation of protected species, installation of best management practices for erosion and stormwater, and commitments to monitoring.

Mitigation costs can be difficult to forecast because agencies may require additional measures after reviewing updated field data or because new regulatory interpretations apply to similar projects. In some cases, we may be required to extend mitigation and monitoring periods beyond the initial scope, increasing ongoing costs. Additionally, adverse weather can affect the success of restoration efforts and delay achievement of required milestones.

If we cannot satisfy mitigation obligations, regulators may impose sanctions, reduce our operating flexibility, or require further corrective actions. In highly regulated locations, mitigation failures may also delay future approvals, which could slow planned capital projects.

While we strive to plan and execute upgrades in a manner consistent with permit requirements, the timing, outcome and financial impact of habitat-related obligations remain uncertain. Any material increases in mitigation costs or project delays could negatively affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Groundwater Availability and Withdrawal Permitting
paragraph_text:
In areas where we rely on groundwater for process needs, our operations depend on water withdrawal permits and compliance with established limits. Permits can require adaptive management plans, metering, reporting and periodic review based on aquifer conditions. If aquifer levels decline faster than expected, regulators may tighten withdrawal limits, require additional monitoring, or reduce permitted extraction rates. Such changes could increase costs for alternative water sources and constrain production.

Additionally, groundwater permits may be subject to renewal risk and may be influenced by municipal or agricultural groundwater usage priorities. Competing users may contribute to drawdown, and regulatory agencies may allocate more restrictive water rights during multi-year drought cycles. If we cannot secure sufficient water supply at commercially reasonable terms, our throughput and customer service levels may be impacted.

We implement groundwater monitoring and water management practices, including maintenance of extraction infrastructure and seasonal operating adjustments. However, monitoring data may not fully capture localized aquifer variability, and mitigation actions required by regulators may be time-consuming to implement. Noncompliance with permit terms could result in enforcement actions, permit revocations, or requirements to undertake corrective measures.

While we seek to manage groundwater risks through proactive engagement with regulators and operational planning, we cannot assure that future regulatory decisions will not materially adversely affect our operations.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Forest Products and Deforestation Due Diligence
paragraph_text:
We use certain wood-derived and paper-based materials in our products and packaging. Our suppliers source these materials from forests and forested regions where deforestation, illegal harvesting or unsustainable land management practices could occur. Even where reputational risks appear limited today, regulatory frameworks and customer programs increasingly require due diligence to demonstrate responsible forestry, protection of water resources and avoidance of conversion of high-conservation-value areas.

If we cannot obtain adequate documentation from suppliers demonstrating compliance with applicable due diligence requirements, we may face contract losses, shipping delays, or additional compliance costs. In some cases, suppliers may not be able to provide traceability information at the level requested, particularly where production is processed through multiple intermediaries.

Furthermore, environmental events such as wildfires, pest outbreaks and extreme drought can reduce available forestry supply, resulting in price volatility and reduced availability. While we manage procurement through diversified sourcing strategies, these strategies may not fully offset localized disruptions.

Any material inability to secure sustainable forest-based inputs, including on a timely basis, could adversely affect our manufacturing schedules, costs and customer relationships.

risk_heading: Risks from Changes in Wetland Mitigation Banking and Restoration Credit Requirements
paragraph_text:
In connection with development activities and infrastructure projects, we may use wetland mitigation banking credits or undertake restoration efforts to offset unavoidable impacts. The availability, cost and eligibility of mitigation credits can vary by region and can change if regulators update credit accounting methods, apply stricter performance requirements, or suspend or revise authorization of certain banks.

If mitigation credits become unavailable or more expensive, we may need to modify project scope, incur additional costs, or seek alternative mitigation solutions with different timelines. Restoration projects can also fail to achieve required ecological performance, which may obligate additional corrective actions, extended monitoring or purchase of replacement credits.

In addition, ecological performance assessments often require multi-year monitoring, and acceptance of credit performance may be delayed. If credit verification occurs later than expected, it may affect financial planning and could potentially result in noncompliance with project permit conditions. Our ability to meet these conditions depends on both the bank’s performance and regulatory acceptance.

While we contract for mitigation in advance and evaluate banks based on historical performance and documentation, outcomes remain uncertain and depend on environmental conditions and regulatory decisions. Any inability to secure acceptable mitigation could delay projects and reduce profitability.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Evolving Land Use and Environmental Screening for New Sites
paragraph_text:
As we expand operations, we evaluate potential sites based on permitting pathways, infrastructure access and environmental suitability. However, environmental screening and due diligence outcomes can vary based on site history, subsurface conditions and the scope of investigations performed. Certain sites may present higher risk of requiring extensive remediation due to historical industrial use, underground storage tanks or legacy contamination.

Land use rules and environmental regulations can change during the acquisition and permitting process. If new restrictions are adopted regarding groundwater protection zones, stormwater infiltration standards, or species and habitat protections, we may need to redesign layouts or incur additional costs to comply. In certain cases, the cost and timing of remediation may cause us to abandon planned projects or delay production.

We may also be subject to additional investigations if regulators or community stakeholders raise concerns about environmental impacts. Even when we proceed with mitigation plans, the effectiveness and timing of remediation efforts can be uncertain, particularly when contaminants are located beneath active infrastructure.

While we seek to mitigate these risks through environmental assessments, engineering controls and insurance where available, we cannot assure that identified risks will not increase or that we will be able to complete site development on commercially reasonable terms. Adverse outcomes could materially affect our capital allocation and operating results.

risk_heading: Risks from Climate-Driven Changes in Water Temperature and Aquatic Resource Health
paragraph_text:
Our operations may use surface water for cooling and process needs. Changes in weather patterns and warming water temperatures can affect cooling system performance and the ecological conditions of receiving waters. Regulators may respond to aquatic ecosystem concerns by tightening discharge limits, requiring additional monitoring, or mandating operational changes during temperature-sensitive periods for aquatic species.

If we are required to reduce intake volumes, modify cooling processes, or install additional cooling or treatment equipment to manage water temperature impacts, our operational costs may increase and production could be constrained. In addition, staffing and scheduling requirements for enhanced monitoring may increase administrative overhead.

We conduct monitoring and maintain cooling infrastructure designed to meet applicable requirements; however, extreme heat events and rapid shifts in water conditions can occur with limited notice. During such events, we may experience higher energy usage, operational constraints or reduced system reliability. Any required shutdowns or curtailments could affect revenue and customer service commitments.

Even if we comply with existing permits, the cost of meeting potential future requirements related to aquatic resource health could be material. Because these rules may be implemented based on emerging science and new regulatory guidance, we cannot predict the extent of future compliance costs or the associated timing of implementation.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Restoration of Disturbed Areas After Construction and Closure
paragraph_text:
Some of our activities, including construction projects and facility expansions, disturb land and can alter drainage patterns and soil stability. When projects are completed or when facilities are partially closed, we are typically required to restore disturbed areas to meet permit and regulatory requirements. Restoration obligations can include grading, re-vegetation, stabilization of slopes, and long-term maintenance.

Restoration outcomes are affected by local climate, soil conditions, availability of native seed or plants, and the occurrence of erosion events. If restoration performance does not meet regulatory expectations, we may be required to implement additional corrective measures, perform replanting, extend monitoring periods or revise stabilization systems. These requirements can continue for multiple seasons and may require the allocation of resources beyond original budgets.

Regulators may update restoration standards over time or require additional studies if vegetation establishment is delayed. Such changes can increase cost and delay the return of disturbed land to its intended condition.

While we follow approved work plans and employ qualified environmental contractors, there can be no assurance that restoration efforts will be accepted without additional actions. Any failure to achieve timely closure and restoration could result in penalties, ongoing monitoring costs and restrictions on future development at the affected locations.

risk_heading: Risks of Increased Operational Costs Due to Water Reuse and Circularity Requirements
paragraph_text:
To manage water scarcity and protect local water resources, regulators and customers may require higher levels of water reuse and more circular water management. In some jurisdictions, permit renewals may include conditions that encourage or mandate increased recycling of process water, tighter controls on effluent discharge, and improved monitoring of reuse systems. While these requirements may align with broader sustainability objectives, they could require substantial investments in reuse infrastructure.

Implementing additional water reuse can increase operational complexity and may require more frequent maintenance, advanced filtration or treatment technologies, and greater attention to scaling, fouling and system reliability. If these systems do not perform as expected—due to variability in influent water characteristics, operational upsets or equipment failures—we could face production disruptions or noncompliance with permit conditions.

We also may need to adjust procurement and operations to reduce reliance on freshwater inputs, which could affect throughput and product quality. Qualifying new treatment chemicals or process parameters may add further costs and time.

We cannot predict the timing, scope or cost of future water reuse requirements. Any material increases in water management-related costs or operational disruptions could adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition.

Permitting for these activities can be complex and may require detailed environmental assessments, seasonal restrictions on work, and commitments to restore or enhance impacted areas. Delays in obtaining permits, challenges to the sufficiency of mitigation plans, or changing interpretations of protected areas could affect project schedules and increase costs.
